unit.title: A Problem on Every Plate
objectives: I can find cause and effect in a text.
I can use the prefix im- to guess word meanings.
I can join two sentences with who, which, or that.

passages.title: Food Waste: A Problem on Every Plate

paragraphs: Every year, roughly one third of the food produced in the world is lost or thrown away. That waste does not happen only in restaurants and supermarkets. A large share of it happens at home, where people buy more than they need, forget leftovers at the back of the fridge, or throw away fruit simply because it looks imperfect.

Wasting food also wastes the water, energy, and labor that were used to grow and transport it. When food rots in landfills, it releases methane, a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere far more effectively than carbon dioxide. In other words, the banana that ends up in the trash has a climate cost as well as a price tag.

Fortunately, small habits can make a real difference. Planning meals before shopping, storing vegetables properly, and understanding that a "best before" date is about quality rather than safety can all reduce waste. Some cities in Taiwan have also introduced food-sharing fridges, where people who have extra food can leave it for neighbors who need it.

Each year, about one third of the world's food is lost or thrown away. This does not only happen in restaurants and shops. A lot of food is wasted at home. People buy too much, forget old food in the fridge, or throw away fruit that looks imperfect.

When we waste food, we also waste the water and energy used to grow it and move it. Old food in the trash makes a gas called methane. This gas makes the Earth warmer. So a banana in the trash costs money and also hurts the climate.

Small habits can help. We can plan meals before shopping. We can keep vegetables in the right place. We can also learn that a "best before" date is about taste, not safety. Some cities in Taiwan have food-sharing fridges. People leave extra food there for neighbors who need it.

glossary.example: We had leftovers from last night for lunch.
The apple is imperfect, but it tastes great.
Most of our trash goes to a landfill.
Methane is a gas that warms the Earth.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
questions.stem_support: What is this text mostly about?

options.text: Food waste is a serious problem, but everyday habits can reduce it.
Supermarkets are the only cause of food waste.
options.feedback: Paragraph 1 says waste does NOT happen only in supermarkets.

options.text: Bananas are more expensive than other fruit.
options.feedback: The banana is just an example in paragraph 2.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1–2 describe the problem; paragraph 3 gives solutions. A covers both. 主旨＝問題＋解決方法。

hints.text: Paragraphs 1 and 2 talk about a problem. What does paragraph 3 talk about?
Key words: "Fortunately, small habits can make a real difference."
Option C is only a small example, not the main idea.
The main idea = problem + solution. Answer: A.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 1, where does a large share of food waste happen?

options.feedback: Farms are not mentioned in paragraph 1.
Schools are not mentioned. Find "a large share" or "a lot of food".

questions.explanation: "A large share of it happens at home."

hints.text: Look at paragraph 1, sentence 3.
Key words: "a large share" / "a lot of food".
words: A lot of food is wasted at home

hints.text: Options A and C are not in the text.
Answer: at home.

questions.stem: Why is food rotting in landfills a climate problem?
questions.stem_support: Why is old food in the trash bad for the climate?

options.feedback: Smell is not mentioned. Which gas does rotting food release?

options.text: It releases methane, which traps heat.
It uses too much carbon dioxide.
options.feedback: Carbon dioxide is only used for comparison. Read the sentence again.

questions.explanation: Cause: food rots → Effect: methane is released → it traps heat in the atmosphere.

hints.text: Go to paragraph 2. Find "When food rots in landfills".
Key words: methane, traps heat.
Option A is not in the text.
Rotting food → methane → heat is trapped. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 3, food that is past its "best before" date ___.

options.text: may still be safe to eat

options.feedback: The text says the date is about quality, NOT safety.

options.text: must be returned to the shop

questions.explanation: If the date is about quality (taste), not safety, the food may still be safe.

hints.text: Find "best before" in paragraph 3.
Key words: "about quality rather than safety".
Option C is not in the text. Is B or A closer to "not about safety"?
Not about safety → it may still be safe. Answer: A.

questions.stem: The store sells ___ vegetables at a lower price because they have strange shapes.

options.feedback: The price is LOWER, so they are not expensive.
Invisible means "cannot be seen". Can you see the strange shapes?

questions.explanation: im- = not; imperfect = not perfect（不完美的）.

hints.text: Why is the price lower? Read the end of the sentence.
The prefix im- means "not". Which word means "not perfect"?
Option B does not fit "lower price".
Answer: imperfect.

questions.stem: Something that is not possible is ___. (Use im-)

hints.text: Start with the word "possible".
Add im- to the front.
im + p... = imp...
Answer: impossible.

questions.stem: Combine the sentences: I have a friend. She volunteers at a food bank.

options.text: I have a friend who volunteers at a food bank.
I have a friend which volunteers at a food bank.
options.feedback: "Which" is for things. A friend is a person.

options.text: I have a friend who she volunteers at a food bank.

questions.explanation: 人 → who；關係代名詞 who 取代 she，所以不能再寫 she.

hints.text: Is "a friend" a person or a thing?
Rule: person → who; thing → which; both → that.
Option B uses which for a person.
Answer: A. who replaces she.

questions.stem: The fridge ___ is next to the library is for sharing food.

hints.text: Is "the fridge" a person or a thing?
Thing → which or that.
Example: The book which I bought is great.
Answer: which (or that).
